plan: With 3 bidders and uniform values on [0,49], the standard first-price auction equilibrium bid is value × (n-1)/n = 32 × 2/3 ≈ 21.3. This balances winning probability against profit margin, shading my bid below true value to maximize expected profit rather than just win probability. I'll bid slightly below this theoretical optimum to account for risk aversion and ensure positive expected profit if I win.

This is effectively a second-price auction: I pay the highest bid among others if I win, not my own bid. In second-price auctions, the dominant strategy is to bid your true value, since bidding higher risks overpaying above my value, and bidding lower risks losing profitable wins. My value is $6, so I will bid exactly that to maximize expected profit.

With 3 bidders and uniform values on [0,49], the optimal first-price auction bid shading factor is (n-1)/n = 2/3. My value is $17, so I should bid approximately 17 × 2/3 ≈ $11.30 to balance winning probability against profit margin. Bidding at or near this level maximizes expected profit given rational competitors likely use similar shading strategies.
